metadataDescription: Fly a spacecraft at true scale from the Moon to the far planets. Real drives, two clocks, the light as it falls there.
canvasLabel: The solar system at true scale, seen from a spacecraft

camera.title: Cockpit view
camera.body: In orbit, the ship holds its view. Take the helm to fly; drag to steer during manual flight.

objects.title: Objects
objects.body: Pick a destination and the autopilot flies there.

drive.title: Drive
drive.body: Each drive takes its own time to get there.

rate.title: Time warp
rate.body: Hold the clocks, or run them faster.

throttle.title: Throttle
throttle.body: Push it to fly the ship by hand.

settings.body: Cockpit, layers and render quality. The camera pad steers during manual flight.

guide.body: Learn what a trip to the stars takes, step by step.

viewHints.earth: Home, from a few radii out. Take the helm to explore.
viewHints.moon: Thirty Earth diameters away. Earth is a small blue disc from here.
viewHints.mars: Sunlight is less than half as strong as on Earth.
viewHints.jupiter: Its moons cast real shadows on the clouds.
viewHints.saturn: The rings, from inside the system.
viewHints.pluto: Noon here is dimmer than Earth's dusk. The Sun is a bright star.
viewHints.stars: Four light-years out, at a sun like ours. The Sun is a bright star behind you.
viewHints.galaxy: Above the disk, two hundred thousand light-years out.
viewHints.andromeda: Two and a half million light-years. On Earth, that many years have passed.
viewHints.edge: Nothing can ever go farther. Galaxies in every direction, none of them mapped.

hud.invite: Fly with W or the lever
hud.keys: W S thrust · A D · R F · Q E roll · Shift boost · X brake · Space orbit · drag to look

bodies.sun: Every surface here is lit from this disc. Its light reaches Earth in eight minutes.
bodies.earth: The only place with liquid water on the surface, and the only one that answers a radio call.
bodies.moon: Its far side never faces Earth. Earth never sets from the near side.
bodies.mars: Half Earth's width; a day forty minutes longer than ours.
bodies.jupiter: Eleven Earths across. Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto pass in front of it and shade its clouds.
bodies.saturn: The rings are mostly water ice, a few tens of metres thick, and would reach three-quarters of the way to the Moon.
bodies.io: The most volcanic world known, squeezed by Jupiter's tides.
bodies.europa: An ocean under the ice, deeper than all of Earth's together.
bodies.titan: A nitrogen sky thicker than Earth's, and lakes of methane.
bodies.pluto: Charon is so large that the pair orbits a point outside Pluto.

far.alphaCen: Two suns {abSeparationAu} au apart, circling each other every {abPeriodYears} years, with Proxima a fifth of a light-year off.
far.proxima: The nearest star to the Sun: a red dwarf, a seventh of the Sun's width, that flares.

technicalDetails.title: How Voyage is drawn
technicalDetails.summary: Every body at its true size and place, in kilometres, with the ship as the scene's origin and a logarithmic depth buffer so a moon's surface and the far planets share one pass. Flights take the drive's real trip time on two clocks. Sunlight falls as the inverse square; moons shade one another in eclipses.

features.scale: The Sun, the planets, the named small worlds and the moons at true size, placed from the JPL elements with the Earth–Moon and Pluto–Charon barycentres resolved.
features.flight: Three drives: Voyager's {voyagerKms} km/s, a light sail at a fifth of light speed, a torch ship at one g that burns, flips at the midpoint and brakes. The autopilot flies the real trip on an automatic time warp; by hand the ship falls in real gravity.
features.clocks: A ship clock and an Earth clock, run at the visitor's rate, that part only when the ship goes fast.
features.light: Sunlight weaker with distance, the light-time home, and eclipses cast by moons and planets.
features.sky: The bright stars at their measured distances and the Milky Way's band, shifting as the ship covers light-years, crowding ahead and changing colour at speed; α Centauri as three suns of their measured size.

scale.title: Positions and scale
scale.body: Bodies sit where the JPL Keplerian elements put them at the moment shown, in kilometres about the Sun; the Moon follows the ELP-2000 lunar theory, good to an arcminute. The Earth–Moon and Pluto–Charon elements place the barycentres, so each planet's centre is moved by the moon's offset times the moon's share of the mass. The ship is the origin of what is drawn; everything is placed by its offset from the ship in double precision, and depth is logarithmic, so a surface a kilometre away and a planet a billion kilometres away keep their order.

flight.title: Flights and clocks
flight.body: A coasting drive takes D / v on Earth's clock and less on the ship's by the Lorentz factor. The torch ship holds its proper acceleration, so each half of the trip is hyperbolic motion: the ship's time is 2(c/a) acosh(1 + aD/2c²). The autopilot first turns onto its route, then plays the trip back in a few seconds: the distance from home grows in even steps of scale, the distance to go shrinks the same way, and at every moment the position, the speed and both clocks are the drive's real ones there; only the playback rate, the time warp the dock shows, is chosen. In orbit, the ship rides with its body and the clocks agree. Flown by hand, the ship leaves orbit at rest beside its body, every drive manoeuvres at one g (the coasting drives no faster than their cruise), and the clocks run at a flight-assist warp that grows with the square root of the height above the nearest surface, so a full burn from rest carries the ship 8 % of that height in two seconds wherever it is. It falls in the gravity of the Sun, the body it is near and that body's planet or largest moon (JPL gravitational parameters), stepped by leapfrog at no less than forty steps per dynamical time; near a body the warp is held back rather than step it coarsely.

light.title: Light
light.body: Each surface is lit from the Sun's position with an inverse-square readout of the sunlight there. Up to four bodies of a surface's own system are tested against the Sun's disc as seen from each point: inside the umbra the Sun is hidden, across the penumbra it is uncovered over the Sun's angular radius, and a disc smaller than the Sun's leaves an annulus lit.

sky.title: The sky from a ship
sky.body: Each catalogue star sits at its SIMBAD parallax distance, so the constellations deform as the ship covers light-years and the Sun fades to a star among them. The Milky Way is the Orrery's painted band, carried with the ship and handed over to the Galaxy map light-years out; its grains and a faint field are painted, not catalogued. α Centauri is drawn as discs: A where the catalogue puts it, B on its measured orbit, Proxima at its own place, each the colour of its temperature. At speed the sky is drawn as the ship sees it: directions crowd toward the direction of travel by the aberration formula, each star's light is shifted by the Doppler factor D, its colour read from a blackbody lookup at D times its Ballesteros temperature, a star's flux raised by D squared, the band's and the background's glow by D to the fourth. Below a thousandth of light speed nothing is changed. Globes too are drawn where a moving ship sees them, their direction aberrated and their width divided by D (a sphere's outline stays a circle), though their light keeps its colour; the Galaxy map alone is drawn where it is. Beyond the mapped structures a field of galaxies drawn round the ship stands for the web no catalogue reaches. A far card says how long the light the ship sees has been under way; the map itself draws every galaxy where it is now. Dust streaming past the ship shows its motion through the near body's frame as seen at the time warp: two lattices of motes a decade apart, blended by that speed, streak longer and brighter the faster the ship goes, and take the Doppler tint near light speed. Past light speed as seen the ship is in cruise, past ten thousand times it in warp: the streaks lengthen and cool, and at warp, the lattice light-years wide, the motes are stars and take blackbody colours, most of them red dwarfs. At true relativistic speed the sky's diffuse light crowds ahead and shifts blue: a glow dead ahead that strengthens with speed. The dust is a cue, not a measurement.

moon.title: The Moon
moon.body: Thirty Earth diameters of nothing. Light crosses the gap in {moonLightSeconds} seconds.

earth.title: Earth
earth.body: A short hop: even at one g the trip takes a few hours of ship time.

mars.title: Mars
mars.body: Months at Voyager's speed, days for the torch ship. Sunlight here is {marsSunlightPercent} % of Earth's.

jupiter.title: Io and Jupiter
jupiter.body: Io's shadow crosses Jupiter every {ioPeriodHours} hours. Radio home: most of an hour.

saturn.title: Saturn
saturn.body: Fly into their plane: ten metres thick, the rings all but vanish.

pluto.title: Pluto
pluto.body: The Sun is a bright star. Set the drive to Voyager and see how long the way back takes.

stars.title: α Centauri
stars.body: The sky has changed: the nearest stars have moved, the Sun is one of them. A and B circle each other in {abPeriodYears} years; Proxima is the red one. Voyager would need {voyagerYears} years. At one g the ship nears light speed within a year and its clock runs slow: {torchAlphaCenYears} years on board, {torchAlphaCenEarthYears} on Earth.

galaxy.title: The Galaxy, from above
galaxy.body: Twenty-four years on board at one g; two hundred thousand on Earth. The Sun is one point in the disk below.

andromeda.title: Andromeda
andromeda.body: Twenty-nine ship years. Earth's calendar has run two and a half million years; the Sun still shines.

edge.title: The edge
edge.body: No ship can go farther: nothing leaving Earth today ever gets beyond this. The microwave background is as far away as from home. It was never a place.
